title: Demonstration of a mobile ion-trap quantum device
authors: Sara Alfaro, Dipesh Bhanushali, Sankarshan Choudapurkar, Ashwin Bhartia, Thomas Lafenthaler, Tommaso Faorlin, Yannick Weiser, Lorenz Panzl, Thomas Monz, Rainer Blatt, Giovanni Cerchiari
abstract: Trapped-ion devices are being investigated for transportable applications, including the transfer of exotic charged particles between laboratories and the development of portable quantum technologies. To date, ion transport has been demonstrated only in magnetic (Penning) traps, whereas radiofrequency (Paul) traps are the predominant platform in quantum science. Here, we report the first transport of a few thousand ions confined in a linear Paul trap over distances of several kilometers, with transport durations of 15 and 45 min. These results establish a foundation for mobile trapped-ion quantum devices capable of operating while in motion and may enable the transport of exotic ions in Paul traps between experimental facilities.
summary: The researchers demonstrated the first successful transport of thousands of trapped ions confined in a linear Paul trap over several kilometers. This achievement establishes a foundation for mobile quantum devices, allowing quantum experiments to be performed while the apparatus is in motion. The work is significant for developing portable quantum technologies and quantum network nodes.
main_problem: The primary goal was to develop a mobile, transportable trapped-ion quantum device capable of operating while in motion, overcoming the limitations of current stationary setups.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated the transport of several thousand ions confined in a linear Paul trap over distances of several kilometers, maintaining storage times consistent with stationary lab measurements.
method: The experiment involved trapping ions in a linear Paul trap, transporting the apparatus over long distances, and detecting the ions using a microchannel plate (MCP) detector after controlled extraction.
model_or_system: The physical system is a trapped-ion quantum device utilizing a radio-frequency linear Paul trap geometry. The system is designed to handle various ion species ($	ext{Be}^+, 	ext{Ca}^+, 	ext{Sr}^+$) and is housed in a transportable rack.
key_observables: Ion count detected via MCP signal, ion storage lifetime ($	au$), and ion retention measured after transport periods (15 min, 45 min).
important_parameters: RF trapping frequency ($\Omega_{RF}$) of $2\pi 	imes 17$ MHz; transport distances of several kilometers; storage times up to 45 minutes.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that the confinement mechanism in the Paul trap remains stable and functional while the entire apparatus is physically moved over long distances.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the experimental setup (Fig. 1), the ion extraction sequence and data processing (Fig. 2), and the ion-transport measurements showing ion counts versus time during movement (Fig. 3).
paper_structure: The paper details the experimental setup, describes the ion generation and detection procedures, presents the results of ion transport over kilometers, and discusses the implications for mobile quantum applications.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the engineering challenge of quantum hardware portability, which is crucial for realizing quantum networks and distributed quantum sensing applications.
